en: The Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra:

Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into dharma for the sake of the supreme good of man. (1) Having known it and practicing it, one is righteous. (2) He becomes most praiseworthy in this world and, after death, attains the heavenly world. (3)

Dharma is that which is prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti. (4) In the absence of that, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is authoritative. (5) Furthermore, the learned person is one whose nature is free from desire. (6) Dharma is that for which no other cause can be apprehended. (7)

To the east of Ādarśa, to the west of Kālakavana, to the north of Pāriyātra, to the south of the Himavat, and to the north of the Vindhya—whatever *dharmas* and whatever customs exist within these limits, all those are to be accepted; but not others whose practices are contrary to this. This region they call Āryāvarta. Some say it is the area between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. Others say that as far as the black antelope roams, so far extends the land of *brahmavarcasa*. Furthermore, the Bhāllavins cite a verse in their Nidāna:
Behind is the Sindhu, the supporter; before is the rising of the sun.
As far as Kṛṣṇa runs, so far indeed extends the splendor of Brahman. ||15||

"Whatever those who are learned in the three Vedas and knowers of dharma declare to be dharma—both that which is purifying and that which is most purifying—that is indeed dharma; there is no doubt about this. (16)
Manu declared that the laws of regions, the laws of castes, and the laws of families are not to be spoken of because they lack scriptural authority.

One who has seen the sun rise while still in bed, one who has seen the sun set while still in bed, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, an elder brother whose younger brother marries first, a younger brother who marries before his elder, a husband whose wife marries before her elder sister, a husband whose younger sister marries before him, one who kills a hero, and one who abandons the Veda—these are sinners. 18.

They declare there to be five great sins (mahāpātaka): violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, killing an embryo, stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, and associating with those who have fallen [from their caste]. This association may be through Vedic study or through marriage. Furthermore, they quote:
"One falls [from caste] by associating with a fallen person for one year, whether through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage; but not by sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food."
One who casts away the sacred fires, one who shows malice toward his teacher, an atheist, one who lives as an atheist, and one who sells Soma—these are secondary sins (upapātaka). 23.

A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives in the order of the castes; a Rājanya, two; and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, one each. (24) Some say that even a Śūdra woman may be taken, provided it is done without the sacred mantras; [but] it is the same [as the previous prohibition]. (25) One should not act in this way. (26) For from this follows the certain degradation of the family, and after death, the exclusion from heaven. (27)

There are six forms of marriage: the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Gāndharva, the Kṣātra, and the Mānuṣa. When one gives a girl to a suitor with a libation of water, that is the Brāhma form. When one gives a daughter, having adorned her, to an officiating priest performing his duties during the course of a sacrifice, they call that the Daiva form. The Ārṣa form consists of giving her along with a pair of cattle. When a man, being desirous, marries a woman of similar birth who is likewise desirous, that is the Gāndharva form. When they carry her away by force after subduing [the opposition], that is the Kṣātra form. When she is obtained by bargaining for wealth, that is the Mānuṣa form. Therefore, it is understood here that a purchase is made when it is said, "A hundred [cows] plus a chariot should be given to the father of the daughter. And it is said in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices: "She who, having been purchased from her husband, then behaves improperly toward others. Furthermore, they also cite this:
Lost knowledge may be regained,
but upon the destruction of a family, there is total ruin;
for even a horse is honored by virtue of its lineage.
Therefore, they marry women of noble birth. ||38||
The three castes shall live according to the instruction of the Brāhmaṇa. (39) The Brāhmaṇa shall proclaim the duties; the king shall enforce them. (40–41)

But a king, ruling according to dharma, shall take a sixth part of the wealth [of his subjects], with the exception of a Brāhmaṇa. For it is said that he partakes of a sixth share of the merit of sacrifices and charitable works. A Brāhmaṇa makes the Veda prosperous; a Brāhmaṇa rescues one from calamity; therefore, a Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten [i.e., not to be taxed]. It is said that Soma is his king.
"And that which pertains to prosperity after death"—thus it is known, indeed, thus it is known. ||46||
Thus ends the first chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
There are four castes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. (1) Three castes are twice-born: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya. (2)
For them,
birth occurs first from the mother, and the second at the binding of the girdle of muñja grass;
here, his mother is said to be the Sāvitrī, and his father is the Ācārya.

"Because he bestows the Veda, they call the teacher 'father'. Furthermore, they cite this: "A man has indeed two kinds of seed for a Brāhmaṇa: that which is above the navel and the other which is below it. That which is above the navel—by means of that, offspring is produced when he initiates Brāhmaṇas, when he teaches them, when he performs sacrifices for them, and when he does what is virtuous. Now, that which is below the navel—by means of that, his own biological offspring is produced here. Therefore, they do not say of a learned man who has studied the Vedas, 'You are childless,' says Hārīta."
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Indeed, no ritual duty belongs to him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
for until he is born in the Veda, he is equal to a Śūdra in his mode of livelihood. (6)
Except for acts involving water and those connected with the *svadhā* offering to the ancestors. ||7||
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying:
"Guard me; I am your treasure.
[Do not give me] to one who is censorious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained."
Do not say "no" to me; may I thus be full of vigor. ||8||
Teach it only to one whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy—
one who would never deceive you in any way.
O Brahmin, tell me to him, for he is the guardian of the treasure.
He who pierces one's ears with that which is not false, causing no pain and bestowing immortality—
him one should regard as both father and mother.
One should not bear malice toward him for any offense whatsoever. ||10||
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their teacher, do not respect him in speech, thought, or deed— just as they are not to be fed by the teacher, so too [is he not to be honored by them].
In that very same way, that sacred learning does not benefit them. ||11||

Just as fire burns dry grass, so does the Veda burn one who questions it without respect; one should not explain the Veda to such a person who shows no honor, for it cannot be mastered by one who lacks reverence. (12)

There are six duties for a Brāhmaṇa: (14) the study of one's own Veda, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts. (15) There are three duties for a Rājanya: (16) study, sacrificing for himself, and giving gifts. (17) Furthermore, protecting the subjects with the sword is his specific duty; he should live by that. (18) These same three [duties] belong to a Vaiśya. (19) Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending [are his means of livelihood]. (20) Service to these [other classes] is the Śūdra’s duty; his mode of life is unrestricted, as are his hair and dress. (21) Or rather, all [classes] may follow an unrestricted mode of life, except for the rule regarding the topknot.
If they cannot subsist by their own duty, they may adopt the next lower occupation, which is more sinful; but never the one that is higher.

Adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, one who lives by trade shall not sell stones, salt, hemp, silk, linen, or skins; nor any dyed woven cloth, nor prepared food, flowers, roots, or fruits; nor perfumes, liquids, water, the juice of medicinal herbs, or Soma; nor weapons, poison, meat, milk and its derivatives, iron, tin, lac, or lead. Moreover, they cite this: "One falls [from one's caste] immediately by selling meat, lac, or salt."
"A Brahmin becomes a Śūdra in three days by selling milk. (27)

Among domestic animals, the single-hoofed ones and those with hair are [forbidden]; likewise, all wild animals, birds, and fanged creatures [are forbidden]. (28) Regarding grains, they say that sesame seeds are [the most significant]. Furthermore, they cite this example:
"Whatever one does with sesame seeds other than eating them, anointing oneself, or giving them as a gift—one becomes a worm and sinks into excrement along with one's ancestors. (30)

Or, at their own will, they may cultivate sesame seeds themselves and sell them; however, there is no such thing as officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, nor accepting prohibited gifts. Furthermore, they cite this:
"The best of the twice-born blaze like fires through their asceticism and oblations;
yet they are extinguished by the acceptance of gifts, just as fires are quenched by water. (31)
Therefore, he should plow with two bulls that have testicles and are uncastrated, before the morning meal. (32) In the summer heat, he should provide them with water. (33)
"The plough, sharp-edged, very auspicious, with a handle for holding the Soma; it digs up the cow, the sheep, and the fat, swelling plant; [it brings] a wagon that carries a chariot. ||34||

The plough is sharp-edged, rich in heroes, well-maned, and possessed of oxen; it is very gracious, with a beautiful nose—for its nose is indeed excellent—by means of its nose it sows, casting [the seed] far away. It has a handle for grasping Soma, for Soma reaches its handle; thus it sows. [It yields] cattle, sheep, goats, horses, mules, and camels, and a fat, beautiful, and excellent young woman.
For how indeed could one plow with a plowshare other than for the purpose of selling grain? ||36||

Flavors may be bartered for flavors, whether they are equal or inferior; however, salt must never be exchanged for other flavors. Sesame, rice, cooked food, knowledge, and persons are also permitted to be exchanged by one who trades.
A Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya shall not practice usury. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who, having purchased grain at a low price, sells it at a high price, is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against usury on a scale;
the killer of an embryo remained steady at the end, while the usurer trembled. (42)

Or they may give it at will to one who has failed in his duties or to a wicked person. (43) Gold [may be increased] twofold, grain threefold. (44) By grain, liquids are likewise explained. (45) So too are flowers, roots, and fruits. (46) [Liquids] weighed on a scale are [increased] eightfold. (47) Now they also cite this: "One may take interest per month of two, three, four, or five percent, according to the order of the social classes. (48)
But the king, through his death, would destroy the increase of wealth;
yet again, through the consecration of a king, the root of wealth increases. (49)
Listen to the rate of interest declared by Vasiṣṭha for a moneylender:
five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; thus the dharma is not violated.
"It does not diminish. ||50||
Thus ends the second chapter of the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Those who have not studied the Vedas, those who do not recite them, or those who maintain no sacred fires, become equal in status to Śūdras. Regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly falls to the state of a Śūdra while still living, along with his descendants."
A Brāhmaṇa does not become a non-reciter of the Ṛgveda, nor a merchant, nor an actor;
nor one who performs service for a Śūdra, nor a thief, nor a physician. (3)
The king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms while being neither observant of vows nor learned in the Vedas; for such a village provides sustenance for thieves. ||4||
Among those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist on their birth alone—even if they have gathered by the thousands—the status of an assembly does not exist. (5)
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of the Dharma, say—that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it. (6)
Whatever four or even three who have mastered the Vedas may declare, that should be known as Dharma, and not the word of thousands of others. //7//
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must always be given only to one learned in the Vedas;
for what is given to one unlearned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities.
Whether a fool is in one's own house or a man of great learning is far away, one should give to the man of great learning; there is no transgression in this. (9)
There is no transgression against a Brahmin who is devoid of the Vedas;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes, having set aside a blazing fire. ||10||
An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied— the three of these are mere bearers of names.
Those kingdoms in which the ignorant eat foods that should be eaten by the learned meet with drought, or a great danger arises. (12)

If a king discovers property that has not been claimed, he shall take it after giving a sixth part to the finder. However, if a Brāhmaṇa who is engaged in the six duties should discover it, the king shall not take it.
Having slain an assassin, they say there is no sin whatsoever for the one who takes his life. Moreover, they cite this example:
"The arsonist, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the one who seizes land or a wife—these six are assassins. (15–16)
One may strike down even an assailant who approaches as an expert in the Vedānta, if he intends to kill; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin. //17//
He who kills an assassin, even if that assassin is born of a noble family and devoted to Vedic study, does not thereby become a killer of an embryo; for it is wrath that meets wrath. (18)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa, one who has performed the four Medha sacrifices, a follower of the Vājasaneyi school, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who continues the lineage of a Brahman-gifted daughter, a Chāndoga, a singer of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, one who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, one who studies the Dharmas, and one whose maternal and paternal lineages for ten generations are known to be Śrotriyas and learned—these are the Snātakas who purify the company at a meal. ||19||

One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences, a reciter of the Dharma, and the three principal ones established in the stages of life—this assembly consists of at least ten members. (20)

But he who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the entire Veda, is an Ācārya (teacher). He who teaches a single portion [of it] is an Upādhyāya (sub-teacher). And he who teaches the Vedāṅgas [is also an Upādhyāya].

A Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms for their own protection or for the protection of the social order; but for a Kṣatriya, that is indeed constant, because his duty is the perpetual protection [of others].

Having washed his feet and hands up to the wrists, he should sit facing either east or north; the sacred place for Brahman (the *brāhma-tīrtha*) is the line to the north of the base of the thumb. With that, he should sip water three times silently. (26) He should wipe his mouth twice. (27) He should touch the cavities [of the head] with water. (28) He should pour water on his head and on his left hand. (29) One should not sip water while walking, standing, lying down, or while bent over. (30)
A Brāhmaṇa [should sip water] that reaches the heart, which is free from bubbles. ||31||
A Kṣatriya [is purified] by water reaching the throat;
a Vaiśya by water that has been sipped; and a woman or a Śūdra by water merely touched.

Even from a small opening, those [streams] which are capable of satisfying the cows [are acceptable]; nor [should one use water] that is corrupted by color, smell, or taste, or that comes from an impure source. ||35–36||

Drops that do not touch the body do not make one impure by leaving a residue. (37) Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, and having sipped water, one should sip water again; likewise, after putting on a garment. (38) And after touching the two lips where there is no hair. (39) There is no defilement from [food] gone into the beard. (40)
Whatever remains stuck between the teeth like a tooth, or whatever may remain inside the mouth after rinsing, one becomes pure by simply swallowing it. (41)
Even for one who is causing others to sip water, the drops that fall upon the ground are declared to be equal [to the earth]; one does not become impure by reason of them. 42.
If, while moving about during meals, he should happen to touch something impure,
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then proceed again.
Whatever may require examination, that he should touch with water. ||44||
Wild deer killed the previous day, fruit fallen by birds, places frequented by children, and that which has been traversed by women. (45)
Whatever merchandise is displayed for sale, and whatever defects exist in the faces of women, are marred by gadflies and flies that settle upon them. (46)
"Prajāpati has declared that all waters situated on the earth and those which provide nourishment to cows are pure, provided they have been thoroughly examined. (47)

Purification for removing stains consists of cleansing with water and earth that which has been smeared with impurities. (48) For objects made of metal, clay, wood, bamboo, and skins, purification is achieved by scrubbing with ashes, burning, planing, and washing, respectively. (49) Objects made of stone and gems are purified like those made of metal. (50) Conch shells and mother-of-pearl are purified like gems. (51) Bone is purified like wood. (52) Ropes, split bamboo, and leather are purified like cloth. (53) Objects made of fruit are purified with cow-hair. (54) Objects made of linen are purified with a paste of white mustard seeds. (55)

The ground attains purity according to the specific nature of the defect through means such as sweeping, scrubbing with cow-dung, scraping, sprinkling, and other implements, each applied to its appropriate place. Furthermore, they cite this: "The ground is purified by four means—by digging, by burning, by scraping, and by being trodden upon by cows—and fifthly, by smearing."
A woman is purified by her menses; a river is purified by its current;
bell-metal is purified by ashes; and copper is purified by acid.
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicating liquors, urine, or feces, or with phlegm, pus, tears, or blood, cannot be purified even by re-firing. (59)
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. 60.
Gold is purified by water alone; likewise is silver. (61-62)

The *daiva* (divine) *tīrtha* is at the base of the little finger; ||64|| that of the *ṛṣis* is on the tips of the fingers; ||65|| that of humans is on the fingertips; ||66|| the *āgneya* (fiery) is in the middle of the palm; ||67|| and the *pitrya* (ancestral) is between the forefinger and the thumb. ||68||

One should say "It is pleasing" when honoring the meals offered in the morning and evening; "It is well-prepared" at rites for the ancestors; and "It is excellent" at rites for auspicious occasions—at rites for auspicious occasions. ||70–71||
Thus ends the third chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||3||
The fourfold caste system is distinguished by innate nature and by specific sacramental rites. ||1||
"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born. Thus also there is a Vedic verse (Nigama). ||2||

He created the Brāhmaṇa with the Gāyatrī, the Rājanya with the Triṣṭubh, and the Vaiśya with the Jagatī; he did not create the Śūdra with any metre at all. Thus, the Śūdra is known to be ineligible for the sacraments. His residence should be among these [three] classes alone.
For all [these], truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, non-violence, and procreation [are essential]. ||4||
"Even in the worship of ancestors, deities, and guests, one should indeed kill an animal"—this is the teaching of Manu. (5)
"In the honey-mixture offering, in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—it is only in these cases that one may kill an animal; not otherwise," so Manu has declared.

For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, in a sacrifice, killing is no different from non-killing.
Moreover, they might cook a large bull or a large goat for a Brahmin, a Kshatriya, or a guest who has arrived, thinking, "In this way we are performing hospitality for him. ||8||
And the water-rites and purification. From the second year onwards, one should perform both for one who has died. According to some, [this applies] from the eruption of teeth.

Having consigned the body to the fire, they enter the water without looking back. (11) Then, remaining right there, they should perform the water-rites with their left hands placed over the right; they should be an odd number and face the south. (12) For the south is indeed the direction of the ancestors. (13) Having gone home, they should remain for three days without eating on a bed of grass. (14) Or they may subsist on what is purchased or what has grown spontaneously. (15)
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives.

The counting of days begins from the time of death. Sapinda-relationship is understood to extend to the seventh generation. (17) For unmarried women, however, it is understood to extend to the third generation. (18) Those who have been given in marriage shall perform [the rites] for others, and they [in turn] for those [relatives]. (19)
The same would apply even to birth for those who desire such subtle purity. (20)
Or [it is due to impurity] because of the seed and the causal factor of the mother and father; ||21|| some say [it is due to the impurity] of the mother alone. ||22|| Furthermore, they cite this:

"There is no impurity for the man during childbirth, provided he does not enter into contact; in that case, it is the menstrual flow that should be known as impure, and that does not exist in the man. ||23||

If that [period] recurs again within the interval, they shall be purified by the remainder [of the current period]. (24) If it occurs during the remainder of a night, they are purified after two nights. (25) If it occurs at dawn, they are purified after three nights. (26) A Brāhmaṇa is purified after ten nights. (27) A Rājanya is purified after fifteen nights. (28) A Vaiśya is purified after twenty nights. (29) A Śūdra becomes pure after one month. Furthermore, they cite this:
"He who has eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or even during his *sūtaka* (birth-impurity)..."
He would go to a terrible hell and be born in the womb of an animal. ||31||
"If a twice-born man eats meat from an animal that has died within ten days, by his own appointment, he becomes a worm at the end of his body and feeds upon its excrement. (32)
It is known from tradition that one becomes purified by studying the Saṃhitā while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months. ||33||

When a child dies before reaching two years of age, or upon a miscarriage, the impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* lasts three nights. Gautama says it is immediate purification. When a person has died in another country, having heard of it after ten days have passed, the impurity lasts one night. If a person who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should die while away from home, Gautama says that after performing the cremation rites again, the impurity is the same as for a corpse.

Having touched a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, dust from a cemetery, a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, or anyone who is impure, one should enter the water for an ablution including the head; "water, water," [so it is said]. //38//
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra. ||4||

A woman is not independent; man is her primary authority. (1) It is known from the sacred tradition that she is neither [to be considered] "without fire" nor "impure during menstruation," for she is immortal. (2) Furthermore, they cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. (3)
The expiation for her husband’s malevolent magic has been declared in the secret [treatises]. ||4||
For month after month, their menstrual flow indeed carries away their misdeeds. ||5||

A woman in her courses remains impure for three nights. She should not apply collyrium; she should not anoint herself; she should not bathe in water; she should sleep on the ground; she should not sleep during the day; she should not touch fire; she should not let go of a rope; she should not clean her teeth; she should not eat meat; she should not look at the planets; she should not laugh; she should not perform any [mundane] action. She should not drink from a broken vessel, but should drink from her cupped hands, or from a vessel that is not broken, or from one made of copper. For it is known: Having slain Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, who had three heads, Indra was seized by evil and thought of himself thus: "I am bound by great unrighteousness. All beings reviled him, crying out, "O slayer of the embryo! O slayer of the embryo! He ran to women, saying, "Accept a third part of this guilt of slaying the embryo for me. They said, "What would happen to us? He said, "Choose a boon. They said, "May we obtain offspring in due season," and "May we unite with our husbands according to our desire until the birth of the child. "So be it," he replied, and they accepted it. This very guilt of slaying the embryo manifests itself month after month [in the form of menses]. Therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman in her courses, for she stands there having assumed the form of the guilt of slaying the embryo. Regarding this, they say: "She must not accept collyrium or ointment, for that is the food of women."
Therefore, they do not feel disgust toward her food, thinking, "May she not come to the sacrifice. ||9||
Those who cohabit with a woman in her courses, those who maintain no sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.
All of them possess the characteristics of Śūdras. ||10||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||5||
"Good conduct is the supreme dharma for all; this is certain.
One whose soul is overwhelmed by deficient conduct perishes both in this world and after death. (1)
Neither austerities, nor sacred knowledge, nor the agnihotra sacrifice, nor ritual fees can ever save this man from falling away, if he has deviated from right conduct. ||2||
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of proper conduct, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences;
at the time of death, the meters abandon such a person.
Like birds whose wings have grown, [they depart] from their nest. ||3||
But for a Brahmin devoid of proper conduct,
what pleasure can the Vedas— the six auxiliary limbs in their entirety along with the sacrifices— be capable of producing?
They are as beautiful to behold as the wife of a blind man. ||4||
The Vedic meters do not save this deceitful person from evil who lives by means of trickery,
even though both syllables are being studied correctly.
That sacred formulation purifies him, just as the rains purify the earth for the sake of nourishment. ||5||
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes of suffering, being diseased and short-lived. (6)
From right conduct dharma bears fruit; from right conduct wealth bears fruit;
through right conduct one attains prosperity; right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is full of faith, and free from envy, lives for a hundred years.
One who knows the Dharma should practice eating, excretion, and movement with great restraint; likewise,
one should exercise restraint over speech, intellect, and vigor, as well as in austerity.
But wealth and longevity must be kept most secret. ||9||
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day, but at night one should do so facing south; by doing thus, one's lifespan is not diminished.
One's wisdom perishes through urinating facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, facing a twice-born man, facing the moon, facing water, or facing the twilight.
One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor in ashes;
nor on cow dung, nor in ploughed land, nor in a sown field, nor on a grassy plot.
Nor in the shade of trees that provide livelihood. ||12||
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the ritual] facing whichever direction is comfortable, as also when there is fear of danger to life. (13)
One should perform ritual acts with water that has been drawn up; bathing may be done even with water that has not been drawn up.
The Brahmin should take earth from the bank that contains sand.
Five kinds of earth should not be taken: that from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, and that which remains after purification has been performed. (17)
One application of clay on the penis, three on each hand—this is remembered as the two-fold [cleansing].
Five applications on the anus, ten on one [hand], and seven on both hands [are prescribed]. (18)
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. (19)
The meal of a sage consists of eight mouthfuls, that of a forest-dweller sixteen, that of a householder thirty-two, and that of a student is unlimited. ||20||
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the draft-ox, and the religious student—these three achieve success only while eating;
for them, there is no success for those who do not eat.
He who is not attached to austerities, gifts, offerings, vows, and observances, nor to the duties of sacrifice and study—that one is beyond action (niṣkriya). ||22||
Yoga, austerity, self-control, charity, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, compassion, knowledge, discernment, and faith—this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa. ||23||
One should know that long-standing enmity, envy, untruthfulness, reviling Brahmins, backbiting, and mercilessness are the characteristics of a Śūdra. 24.
Those who are peaceful and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, who have desisted from killing living beings,
and whose hands are restrained from accepting gifts—
Those brahmins are capable of delivering [others]. ||25||
One vessel consists of the Vedas, and another vessel consists of austerity;
yet the most excellent of all vessels is he in whose stomach the food of a Śūdra does not reside.
Any twice-born man who dies with the food of a Śūdra still in his stomach shall become a village pig or be born into that man's family. (27)
For one whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, even if he constantly studies, performs fire-sacrifices,
or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher state.
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra—his sons belong to the one whose food it was, and he himself shall not be worthy of heaven. (29)
One who is rich in Vedic study, of noble birth, tranquil, established in the sacrificial rites, fearful of sin, possessed of great knowledge,
patient toward women, righteous, and a refuge for cows—
They say such a person, exhausted by vows, is a worthy recipient. ||30||
Just as milk, curd, ghee, or honey placed in an unbaked clay vessel would be destroyed due to the weakness of the vessel—both the vessel and those liquids being ruined—so it is here. (31)
In this way, an ignorant person who accepts a cow, gold, clothing, a horse, land, or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes like wood.

One should not practice fingernail-clapping on a woman. (33) Nor [should one do so] with the nails on a vessel or similar object. (34) One should not drink water with cupped hands. (35) One should not strike water with a foot or a hand. (36) Nor [should one strike it] with water against water. (37) One should not knock fruit down with bricks. (38) Nor [should one do so] with fruit against fruit. (39)
One should not be deceitful nor fraudulent. (40) One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas. (41) Furthermore, they cite this:
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes; nor should one be fickle with speech or limbs—such is the sphere of conduct for the cultured. (42)

Those for whom the Veda, along with its auxiliary expansions, has been handed down through tradition, are to be known as cultured Brahmins; they are the authorities for the Vedas and direct perception. (43)
He whom no one knows as existent or non-existent, as unlearned or deeply learned, as well-behaved or ill-behaved— he is a brāhmaṇa.
"He is a Brahmin. ||44||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||6||

There are four stages of life (āśramas): [1] the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka). [2] Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, and having remained firm in his vow of celibacy (brahmacarya), he may enter whichever of these he desires. [3]
The student shall serve his teacher until the liberation from the body [i.e., death]. When the teacher has died, he shall serve the fire; for it is known: "The fire is indeed your teacher."

Restrained in speech; [89] eating at the fourth, sixth, or eighth meal-time of the day; subsisting on alms; dependent upon the teacher; [11] wearing matted hair, or having a single lock of matted hair.

He should follow the teacher when he is walking; if the teacher is sitting, he should remain standing; if the teacher is lying down, he should remain seated while attending upon him. (12) He should study only when summoned. (13) Having offered everything he has obtained, he should eat with the teacher’s permission. (14)

He shall avoid beds, couches, cleaning the teeth, collyrium, and ointments. (15) He shall stand during the day and sit during the night. (16) Three times a day he shall approach water, saying "Water! Water! (17)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

A householder, having subdued anger and joy and being authorized by his teacher, shall bathe and take a wife who is of the same *ṛṣi* lineage, has not yet experienced sexual intercourse, is younger than himself, and is of equal status. (1) She should be fifth from her maternal relatives and seventh from her paternal relatives. (2) He shall kindle the nuptial fire. (3)
One should not turn away a guest who has arrived in the evening. No one should dwell in his house without eating.
If a Brahmin seeking lodging comes to one's house and does not eat, he departs taking away whatever merit that person has accumulated. (6)
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for an indefinite period, he is therefore called a guest. ||7||
A Brahmin guest from another village, as well as one who has arrived by chance, shall not stay in the house without eating, whether he arrives at the proper time or at an improper time. 8.

One who is faithful by nature and free from covetousness is capable of maintaining the sacred fires; he should not fail to establish the fires. (9) And he is capable of performing the Soma sacrifice; he should not fail to be a performer of the Soma sacrifice. (10)

He should be devoted to Vedic study, sacrifice, and procreation. He should honor a guest who has arrived at his house by rising from his seat, offering a seat, speaking kind words, being free from envy, and providing food according to his ability to all living beings.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity. Among the four stages of life, the householder is indeed preeminent. (14)
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their resting place in the householder. 15.
Just as all living beings live by depending on their mother, so do all mendicants live by depending on the householder. ||16||

One who constantly uses water for purification, always wears the sacred thread, constantly engages in Vedic study, avoids the food of outcasts, approaches his wife during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules— [such a person is not defiled].
A Brahmin does not fall from the world of Brahmā.
"From the Brahma-world," [it is said]. ||17||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.

The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) shall wear his hair matted and be clothed in rags or skins. (1) He shall not enter a village. (2) He shall not stand upon ground tilled by the plow. (3) He shall gather roots and fruits that have not been cultivated. (4) His vital energy shall be drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas). (5) His disposition shall be one of patience. (6) He shall honor a guest who has arrived at his hermitage with alms consisting of roots and fruits. (7) He may indeed give, but he shall not accept gifts. (8) He shall perform ritual ablutions with water three times a day. (9)

Having established the sacred fire according to the *śrāmaṇaka* rite, he becomes one who maintains the consecrated fire (10). After six months, he should dwell at the foot of a tree, without fire and without a fixed dwelling (11). He should make offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings;
he shall go to the eternal heaven—thus it is called "the eternal" (12).
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.
The wandering mendicant should depart after having bestowed the gift of fearlessness upon all beings. Furthermore, they cite this:
"For that sage who wanders having granted fearlessness to all beings, there shall never be any fear from any being."
But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his vow, kills both those born and those unborn, and seizes the property of him to whom he gave protection. (3)
One may renounce all ritual actions, but one must not renounce the Veda;
by renouncing the Veda, one becomes a Śūdra; therefore, one must not renounce the Veda. ||4||
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;
begging is superior to fasting; and compassion excels giving. ||5||
Shaven-headed, without "mine-ness," and without possessions; he should go for alms to seven houses without prior intention. [He should do so] when the smoke has ceased and the pestle is laid aside.
He wears a single garment (*ekaśāṭī*) [9], or else an antelope skin (*ajina*) [10]. His body is covered with grass cut by cows, and he sleeps on the bare ground (*sthaṇḍilaśāyin*) [11].

He should dwell in an impermanent abode (12)—at the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree (13). Studying knowledge with the mind (14), he should be constantly in the forest (15). He should not wander about when domestic animals are in sight (16). Moreover, they quote this:
"For one who is constantly in the forest and has conquered his senses..."
"For one who turns away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind has reached inward reflection, and who is equanimous, there is indeed certain non-returning. ||17||
He whose outward signs are unmanifest and whose conduct is unmanifest; he who is not insane, yet wears the garb of a madman. Moreover, they cite this:
"There is no liberation for one devoted to the science of grammar, nor for one delighted in winning over the world."
Not for one intent on food and clothing, nor even for one fond of beautiful dwellings. ||20||
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by giving instructions or prophetic utterances. (21)

One should not be despondent in the absence of gain, nor should one rejoice in its presence; one should possess only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, having emerged from attachment to material requisites. (22)
He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three sacrificial fires;
nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he indeed is a knower of liberation. //23//
Or he may eat what he obtains from a Brahmin family in the evening and in the morning, excluding honey and meat; yet he should not eat to satiety.

Or he may live in a village. (26) He should be straightforward, free from guile, and not fickle. (27) He should not engage in sensory contact with anyone. (28) He should be equanimous toward all living beings. (29)

The avoidance of slander, envy, arrogance, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, reviling others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and malice is held to be the duty for all stages of life. (30) A Brāhmaṇa who wears the sacred thread, carries a water-pot in his hand, remains pure, and avoids the food of a Śūdra, does not fall from the world of Brahman—no, he does not fall from the world of Brahman. (31)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.
There are six who are worthy of the guest-offering (argha): the officiating priest, the bridegroom, the king, the paternal uncle, the Snātaka, and the maternal uncle. ||2||

One should offer oblations into the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) morning and evening from the prepared *vaiśvadeva* food. (3) One should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) to the household deities (*gṛhadevatā*). (4) Having given the first portion to a learned *śrotriya* or to a student (*brahmacārin*), one should thereafter give to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (5) Then one should feed the guest (*atithi*), beginning with the most distinguished and proceeding in order of merit. (6) Among the members of one’s own household, these include maidens, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth. (7) After that, one should feed other members of the household. (8) One should scatter food on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, outcasts (*patita*), and crows. (9) One may give the remains of the meal (*ucchiṣṭa*) or even food that is not the remains (*anucchiṣṭa*) to a *śūdra*. (10) The husband and wife should eat what remains; however, if everything has been consumed, cooking must be performed again. (11)
If a guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has already been set out, one should specially prepare food for him. They bring water for a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived as a guest; for it is known:
"The Vaiśvānara enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest;
therefore they bring water."
Except during the rainy season—people know that peace as such. ||13||
Having fed him, one should attend upon him. Then, one should follow him as he departs as far as the boundary, or until he has given permission.

On the afternoon of the day after the fourth [lunar day], one should offer [the śrāddha] to the ancestors. (16) Having assembled on the preceding day Brāhmaṇas who are ascetics, householders, or virtuous men of mature age, who do not persist in improper acts, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and who are neither pupils nor resident students; (17) one may also feed pupils provided they possess good qualities. (18) One must exclude those who are naked, those with white hair, eunuchs, the blind, those with black teeth, those with leprosy, and those with deformed nails. (19) Furthermore, they cite this: "If one is skilled in the mantras, even if he is afflicted by bodily defects that defile the row, Yama has declared him to be blameless; indeed, he is a sanctifier of the row. (20)
At a Śrāddha ceremony, the remnants of the food must not be removed until the end of the day;
for streams of nectar drip from them, and those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink from them. (21)
One should not wipe away the remnants [of the offering] until the sun has set;
thereafter, inexhaustible streams of milk flow for those who participate in the circumambulation.

"According to the Vedic revelation, for those who have died before the performance of the sacraments, as well as for those with servants, Manu has declared both the leavings of food and the scrapings from the dish to be their share. (23)
One should discard on the ground for those who have not yet departed—the remnants, the scattered grains, the smearings, and the water-offerings—for those who are childless and short-lived. (24)
When food has been offered to the ancestors and set down upon both branches, the evil-minded asuras wait for that interval. (25)
Therefore, a wise man, when food has been brought to him, should receive it with an empty hand; or, having touched his vessel, he may stand until the remnants have been cleared away. (26)
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two; even if very wealthy, one should not be intent upon a large company.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the brahmins—these five things are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it. (28)
Or alternatively, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed?
Having set aside a portion of all the food prepared into a vessel— ||30||
Having performed [the rites] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the *śrāddha*;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*). //31//
As long as the food is warm, as long as they eat with speech restrained,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned, so long do the ancestors eat.
The qualities of the sacrificial offering should not be described as long as the ancestors have not been satiated;
once the ancestors have been satiated, the excellence of the offering may then be spoken of.
But an ascetic appointed to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods who should discard meat shall fall into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body. (34)
Three things are purifying at a funeral feast: a daughter's son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds.
And three things they praise here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste. (35)
When the sun becomes dim in the eighth part of the day, that time is known as *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible. (36)
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having performed a *śrāddha* and having eaten [at it], his ancestors become consumers of semen for that entire month. (37)
The child born from that [woman], having given and consumed what belongs to the father, does not attain knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan. (38)
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather, wait upon the son who is born, just as birds wait upon the peepul tree. (39)
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—this man will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the asterism Maghā. (40)
The ancestors rejoice in a son who increases the lineage, who is diligent in the duties toward his father, and who is devoted to the gods and the Brahmins. (41)
His ancestors rejoice like farmers at a bountiful rain when he, staying at Gayā, offers food; by that act, his ancestors truly possess a son. (42)

One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, and also on the Anvaṣṭakā day. (43) There is no restriction regarding substance, place, or time, provided that Brāhmaṇas are present. (44)

A Brāhmaṇa must necessarily establish the sacred fires (agnyādheya). He must also perform the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice. For this is a constant obligation and is praised as a debt. Indeed, it is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: he owes a sacrifice to the gods, offspring to the ancestors, and a life of studentship to the seers. Thus, one who has sacrificed, who has fathered a son, and who has lived as a student is free from debt.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception; a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception; and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception.

The staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of *pālāśa* wood; or that of a Kṣatriya may be made of *naiyyagrodha* wood; or that of a Vaiśya may be made of *audumbara* wood. The staff of a Brāhmaṇa reaches as high as his hair; that of a Kṣatriya reaches as high as his forehead; that of a Vaiśya reaches as high as his nose. The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of *muñja* grass; that of a Kṣatriya is a bowstring; that of a Vaiśya is made of hempen threads. The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa is a black antelope skin; that of a Kṣatriya is the skin of the *raurava* deer; that of a Vaiśya is the skin of a cow or a goat. The garment of a Brāhmaṇa is white and unwashed; that of a Kṣatriya is dyed with madder; that of a Vaiśya is dyed with turmeric or made of silk. Or, for all of them, it may be a woven garment that is not dyed.

A Brāhmaṇa should beg for alms with "bhavat-pūrvām" (placing *bhavat* at the beginning). A Rājanya [Kṣatriya] should do so with "bhavan-madhyām" (placing *bhavat* in the middle). A Vaiśya should do so with "bhavad-antyām" (placing *bhavat* at the end).

The time for a Brāhmaṇa has not passed until the sixteenth year; for a Kṣatriya, until the twenty-second; for a Vaiśya, until the twenty-fourth. Beyond this, they become those who have lost their right to the Sāvitrī. One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor perform sacrifices for them, nor should one have marriages contracted with them.

One whose *sāvitrī* has fallen [due to the lapse of the initiation age] shall perform the *uddālakavrata*: for two months he should subsist on barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), for one month on milk, for half a month on curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*), for eight nights on clarified butter, for six nights on food obtained unasked, for three nights on water, and he should fast for one day and night. Or he may go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice; or he may perform the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice—yes, he may perform it.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

Now, therefore, follow the observances of a Snātaka. (1) He should not beg from anyone except for a king or a pupil. (2) If overcome by hunger, however, he may beg for something—either what has been prepared or what has not—be it a field, a cow, goats or sheep, or, at the very least, gold, grain, or food. (3) The instruction is that a Snātaka must not perish from hunger. (4)

One should not live with one who wears soiled clothes; ||5|| nor with one who is menstruating; ||6|| nor with one who is unfit [for intercourse]. ||7|| One should not be a "family-to-family" man (one who marries into the same family). ||8|| One should not step over a stretched-out calf-rope. ||9|| One should not look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun. ||10||

One should not void urine or feces in water (11). One should not spit (12). Having wrapped one’s head and having covered the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice, one should void urine and feces, facing north during the day and facing south at night; one should sit facing north during the two twilights (13). Now they also quote: "For those who have completed their Vedic studies, there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper one, two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water" (14).
Fire is said to be pure in water, in the hand, and in wood;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water.
For Manu Prajāpati has declared this to be the "circumambulation with fire" (paryagnikaraṇa);
having performed the necessary duties, one who is most skilled in purification should sip water for rinsing. Thus [ends the section]. 17.
One should eat food facing the east. (18) One should swallow the entire morsel silently with the thumb. (19) And one should not make a sound with the mouth. (20)
He should approach his own wife during her season, avoiding the forbidden days. He should not go to a non-tīrtha woman. Furthermore, they cite this:
"But he who performs sexual intercourse in the mouth of his wedded wife—his ancestors become consumers of semen for that month."
That delight which arises from non-transgression is rooted in the Dharma. ||23||
Moreover, it is known from the *Kāṭhaka*: "May those among us who are to be born tomorrow lie with their husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra. (24)

One should not climb a tree. (25) One should not descend into a well. (26) One should not blow on a fire with one's mouth. (27) One should not pass between a fire and a Brāhmaṇa. (28) Nor between two fires. (29) Nor between two Brāhmaṇas, unless one has first obtained their permission. (30) One should not eat together with one's wife; for it is known in the Vājasaneyaka that [if one does so] the offspring will be lacking in vigor. (31) One should not point out a rainbow by its name. (32) One should call it "the jewel-bow" (maṇidhanus). (33)

One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick [made of that same wood]. (34) One should not eat while holding food on one's lap. (35) One should not eat while sitting on a bench. (36)

He should carry a staff made of bamboo (37). And he should wear two golden earrings (38). He should not wear a garland in public, except for one made of gold (39). He should avoid assemblies and social gatherings (40). Now they also quote:
"Disregard for the Vedas, contempt for the sages, and a lack of discipline in all matters—this is the destruction of the self" (41).

One should not go to a sacrifice if it is unenclosed; if one must go, one should return by the same path, keeping it to the right. (42) One should not set out on a journey when the sun is directly over the tops of the trees. (43) One should not board a boat that is in a precarious state. (44) One should not cross a river with one's arms alone. (45) Having risen during the latter part of the night to study, one should not lie down again. (46) During the *prājāpatya* muhūrta, a Brāhmaṇa should observe certain restrictive rules; he should observe them, indeed, he should observe them. (47)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.

Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (*svādhyāyopākarma*). On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, having established the sacred fire, he offers oblations of uncrushed grains (*akṣatadhānā*). [He offers] to the gods, to the seers (*ṛṣi*), and to the meters (*chandas*). Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing and having consumed curds, they may then commence their Vedic studies.
For four and a half months, or five and a half months. After that, he should study during the bright fortnights. However, he may study the Vedāṅgas at will.

His periods of non-study are as follows: during the twilights when there is thunder; during the twilights [in general]; in cities where a corpse is present or which are designated for public proclamation; at will, however, on ground that has been smeared with cow-dung or swept clean; at the edge of a cemetery; while lying down; and for one who has participated in a *śrāddha* ceremony. Regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, food, or whatever else may be part of a *śrāddha*, there is no study; for Brāhmaṇas are traditionally said to have their hands as their mouths."

[One should not study] while running, when there is a foul odor and so forth, or on barren soil (17); when one has climbed a tree (18); nor on a boat or in an army (19); nor after eating while the hands are still wet (20); nor when the sound of an arrow is heard (21); nor on the fourteenth day, the new moon day, the eighth day, or during the *aṣṭakā* festivals (22); nor when one’s feet are extended or when one is supported by another with the lap (23); nor in the presence of a teacher (24); nor on a bed that has been used for sexual intercourse (25); nor with a garment that has been used for sexual intercourse and has not been washed (26); nor at the edge of a village (27); nor when one has vomited (28); nor when one has urinated or defecated (29).

And [one should not study] when the *Ṛgveda* or *Yajurveda* is being recited, or when the word "Sāman" is heard; ||30|| when there is indigestion; ||31|| during a thunderclap; ||32|| during an earthquake; ||33|| and during an eclipse of the moon or sun. ||34||

In the case of the falling of mountains, the crashing of peaks, or rains of stones, blood, and dust, the impurity lasts for the duration of that event. (35) When there is a conjunction of meteors and lightning, the impurity lasts for three nights. (36) A meteor accompanied by lightning and its radiance [is treated as such]. (37) If this occurs outside the rainy season, the impurity lasts for the duration of that event. (38) Upon the death of a teacher (*ācārya*), the impurity lasts for three nights. (39) Upon the death of a teacher’s son, a pupil, or a wife, the impurity lasts for one day and night. (40)

One should rise and salute the officiating priest, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle when they are not younger than oneself. (41) And likewise, one should salute the wives of those who are to be saluted by touching their feet, as well as the wife of one's teacher. (42) And also one's mother and father. (43)

He who knows [the rules] should say "I am here, sir" (*aham ayam bho*) when being greeted. And he who does not know [them]... [45] ...when being addressed for a return-greeting, his final vowel undergoes prolation; a *saṃdhyakṣara* (diphthong) that is not *pragṛhya* becomes *āy*, as in "bho bhāvi" [for "bho bhavati"]. [46]

A father who has fallen [from his caste] is to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall toward her son. Furthermore, they cite this: "The teacher is ten times more venerable than the sub-teacher; the father is a hundred times more venerable than teachers; the mother exceeds the father a thousandfold in respect. (48)
A wife, sons, and disciples who have become associated with evil deeds should be rebuked and then abandoned; he who abandons them otherwise [for no such reason] is fallen.
A sacrificial priest and a teacher who fail to officiate at sacrifices or teach should be abandoned; otherwise, by failing to abandon them, one falls from his status. 50.
They say that one who is born from an outcast becomes an outcast, with the exception of a woman; for she belongs to another. He may approach her without inheriting her property.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one’s conduct toward him is desired to be the same as toward the teacher;
according to the sacred tradition, one should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher himself.

Weapons, poison, and liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa. (55) Learning, wealth, age, kinship, and ritual action are grounds for respect. (56) Each preceding one is more weighty than the following. (57)

When [these] meet on a path, way must be yielded one after another: to an elder, to one who is ill, to one burdened with a load, to a woman, and to a king’s chariot. (58) When a king and a *snātaka* meet, way must be yielded by the king to the *snātaka*. (59) Way must be yielded by everyone to a bride being carried away. (60)
Grass, ground, fire, water, kind speech, truthfulness, and freedom from envy—these are never cut off in the house of the virtuous, never at any time. ||61||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.

Now, therefore, we shall describe what is fit and what is unfit to be eaten. The food of a physician, a hunter, an unchaste woman, a magistrate, a thief, one accused of a crime, a eunuch, and an outcast is not to be eaten. (2) Nor that of a miser, one initiated for sacrifice, a prisoner, a sick person, a seller of Soma, a carpenter, a washerman, a distiller of spirits, an informer, a usurer, and a leather-cutter. (3) And [the food] of a Śūdra. (4) And of one who bears arms. (5) Of a paramour, and of one who considers himself a paramour. (6) And of one who sets fire to houses. (7) And of one who does not execute those deserving of death. (8) And that which is called out for, "Who will eat this? (9) The food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan. (10) Moreover, they cite this:
The gods do not eat the food of one who keeps a dog, nor of the husband of a low-caste woman; they do not eat the food of one conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house lives a paramour. ||11||

He may accept fuel, water, fodder, *kuśa* grass, parched grain, food offered for him, a vehicle, a dwelling, a carp, *priyaṅgu* seeds, garlands, perfumes, honey, and meat—these he may accept. Moreover, they cite this:

"One who wishes to support his wife for the sake of his guru, or one who intends to honor the gods and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; yet he himself shall not satisfy his own appetite with them."

The food of a hunter who roams with arrows is not to be avoided. For it is known that Agastya engaged in hunting during a thousand-year sacrificial session (*sattra*); the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) for him were made from the flesh of excellent wild animals and birds at the time when no other provisions were available. Moreover, in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"Prajāpati considered alms-food—even if offered by an evildoer—to be fit to be eaten, provided it is brought forward spontaneously and was not solicited beforehand. (14–16)
One may eat the food of even a thief, provided he is full of faith,
but never that of one who performs many sacrifices for hire, nor of one who initiates many pupils.
Neither do his ancestors eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblation, for him who treats her with contempt.
Even when offered, [a gift] is not accepted from a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a fisherman, a eunuch, or an unchaste woman. ||19||

The leavings of one who is not one's teacher are unfit to be eaten. (20) One's own leavings, as well as food defiled by the leavings of others, are unfit to be eaten. (21) So too is that which has been defiled by clothing, hair, or insects. (22) However, having removed the hair and insects, sprinkled it with water, or scattered ashes over it, one may use such food if it is commended by word. (23) For on this matter they cite these verses of Prajāpati: "The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen [by insects], that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word. (24)
In a temple courtyard, at weddings, and during sacrifices that have been commenced,
one should not discard food that has been touched by crows or dogs.
Therefore, having set aside a portion of the food, the remainder deserves purification:
by pouring liquid over it for fluids, but by sprinkling for solids.
For that which has been touched by the mouth of a cat shall indeed remain pure. ||27||

Food that is stale, tainted by its nature, containing insects, re-cooked, raw, or cooked in a frying pan [should not be eaten]. (28) However, one may consume it if it has been sufficiently sprinkled with curd or clarified butter. (29) For in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"Whether it be ghee or oil, a Brahmin must not eat what has fallen from his fingernails;
Yama declared that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow's flesh. (30)
But those fats, salts, and condiments which are given with the hand do not reach the giver; the eater consumes only sin. (31)
Therefore, one should give what is to be given using an intermediary, and with a leaf or with wood;
one should never give with the bare hand, nor ever with an iron vessel. ||32||

For eating garlic, onions, leeks, *gṛñjana*, the resin of the *śleṣmātaka* tree, blood, meat cut with a knife, food licked by dogs or crows, or the remnants of a Śūdra’s meal, an *atikṛcchra* penance is required; for other such things, except for honey, meat, and products made from fruit, a *kṛcchra* penance is required. (33) One should avoid the milk of a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*), the milk of a cow whose calf has not yet been born, and the milk of cows, buffaloes, or goats within ten days of calving. (34–35) One should avoid water from a boat crossing a river. (36) One should avoid cakes, fried grains, *karambha*, parched barley flour, stuffed cakes, oil, milk-rice, and vegetables that have turned sour. (37) And one should avoid other products made from milk or ground barley. (38)

The porcupine, the hedgehog, the rabbit, the tortoise, and the iguana are among the five-toed animals that may be eaten. (39) Among domestic animals, those other than the camel and those with teeth only on one side [may be eaten]. (40)

Or among fish, there are the ceṭa, gavaya, śiśumāra, crocodile, and crab; ||41|| those of deformed shape and those with serpent-like heads; ||42|| as well as the white cow, the gavaya, and the śarabha; ||43|| likewise, those not specifically mentioned [as fit for sacrifice]; ||44|| and cows and bulls whose teeth have fallen out. ||45||
In the Vājasaneyaka, it is known that the cow and the ox are fit for consumption and are pure. Regarding the rhinoceros and the non-domestic pig, however, there are differing opinions.

And among birds, there are the raptors, the grain-scatterers, and the web-footed; the *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the *haṃsa*, the *cakravāka*, the *bhāsa*, the crow, the pigeon, the *kurara*, the *sāraṅga*; the white dove, the *krauñca*, the *krakara*, the *kaṅka*, the vulture, the hawk, the *baka*, the crane, the *madgu*, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the *māndhāla*, the night-prowler, the woodpecker, the sparrow, the *railātaka*, the *hārītaka*, the wagtail, the domestic cock, the parrot, the *sārikā*, the cuckoo, and the carnivorous scavengers; and those that frequent villages, and those that frequent villages. Thus [ends section 48].
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
A person is produced from blood and semen, having the mother and father as their cause. (1) Regarding his giving away, selling, or abandoning, the mother and father have authority. (2)

But one should neither give away nor accept an only son; for he is intended for the continuation of the lineage of the ancestors. Nor should a woman give away or accept a son without the permission of her husband.

One who intends to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen, announce it to the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* formulas in the middle of the house, he should adopt one whose kin are distant and who is not closely related. (6) And when a doubt arises, he should treat him as a Śūdra, since he is a distant relative. (7) For it is known from scripture that by means of one person, many may be saved. (8)

If, after he has been adopted, a legitimate son (aurasa) is born, the adopted son shall be entitled to a fourth share, provided that he is not disqualified from participating in the rites for prosperity (abhyudayika). ||9–10||

11. A defiler of the Vedas, a priest for Śūdras, and those who have fallen from the ranks of the highest caste—these are the ones for whom the pouring out of the full vessel (pātraninayana) is prescribed. 12. Having taken a vessel that is not complete from the refuse heap, a slave, or the son of a woman of a different caste, or a kinsman, or one who is dissimilar and devoid of good qualities, shall spread out Darbha grass with its tips pointing forward or red-colored grass with his left foot, and pour out the full vessel for him. 13. And his relatives, with their hair disheveled, shall touch the person who pours it out. 14. Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), they may enter their houses at will. 15. From this time forward, they shall not treat him according to the law. 16. Those who follow his [former] practices and continue to treat him according to the law [are themselves liable].
But for those who have fallen [from their status] yet have performed the vow, there is a restoration. Now they also cite this: "He who restores first shall go as if playing and laughing;
he who causes one to fall later shall go as if grieving and weeping. (17–18)
Those who have killed their preceptor, mother, or father [are purified] through his grace or by means of banishment. ||19||

This is their restoration: having filled a golden vessel or one made of clay with water from a full pool or a flowing stream, they sprinkle him with those waters while reciting the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses. All the rites for the restoration of one who has been consecrated are explained by the [rites] for the birth of a son; they are explained.‖20–21‖
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Now, concerning legal proceedings: ||1|| The king or the minister shall conduct the affairs of the court. ||2|| When two parties are disputing, he shall not take the side of either one. ||3||

For there is indeed no offense according to the seat; at the end, there is no offense. [He who is] equal toward all beings—there is indeed no offense according to the seat, for the first two classes [of letters] up to the end of knowledge.

And one should protect what has been acquired. ||6|| [This applies to] the wealth of kings and minors. ||7|| [Also for] those who have not yet attained legal capacity. ||8|| But when the time has arrived, that which belongs to them [should be restored]. ||9||
A written document, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the three kinds of evidence;
by means of these, the creditor shall first recover his wealth. ||10||
There is emission from the paths and fields, as well as their transformation; [this occurs] for a distance of three paces within the courtyards and streets of young houses. ||11-12||

In a dispute over a house or field, the testimony of the neighbors is authoritative. (13) In a dispute among neighbors, the testimony of written records is authoritative. (14) In a dispute regarding written records, the testimony of the elders and guilds of the village or city is authoritative. (15) Furthermore, they cite this example:

"That which is inherited from a father, that which is purchased, that which is received as a gift, that which is received as a dowry, that which is obtained through marriage, that which is acquired by trade, and likewise that which is obtained by clearing a forest—these are the eight kinds of title. (16)
In that regard, [the period of] ten years applies to property that has been used and then abandoned. Furthermore, they cite this:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, a sealed deposit, women, royal property, and the wealth of a Vedic scholar are not lost through adverse possession. (18)
The confiscated goods shall go to the king. Otherwise, the king, together with his ministers and the citizens, shall carry out the legal proceedings. ||19–20||

Either the king is superior to the creator [of his retinue], and he may have a retinue of vultures; or the king is superior, and he may have a retinue of vultures; or there may be a retinue of vultures, but not a king who is a vulture with a retinue of vultures. For faults arise from a retinue, as does the destruction of theft and plunder. Therefore, one should inquire about the retinue beforehand.
Now, concerning witnesses: ||27|| A witness should be one who is learned in the Vedas, handsome, virtuous, meritorious, and truthful. ||28||
Either all [the causes] exist in all [the effects], or [all the effects arise] from all [the causes]. ||29||
For women, witnesses should be women; for the twice-born, similar twice-born men;
for Śūdras, virtuous Śūdras; and for those of the lowest castes, those born of the lowest wombs. ||30||
Moreover, they cite this example:
"A son is not liable to pay for a suretyship, a frivolous debt, what is owed for gambling, what is owed for liquor, or the remainder of a fine or a tax. (31)
Speak the truth, O witness; your ancestors hang suspended, rising up and falling down as they await your word. (32)
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, hungry and thirsty, and blind, he who gives false testimony shall go to the house of his enemy as a beggar. (33)
One kills five by lying about a maiden; one kills ten by lying about a cow;
one kills a hundred by lying about a horse; one kills a thousand by lying about a human being. (34)
When her husband has died in legal proceedings, expiation for a woman of good family occurs;
their previous associations are severed here by those who offer rebukes. (35)
At the time of marriage, during sexual union, when life is at stake, or when all one's wealth is being seized—
one may indeed speak untruth for the sake of a Brahmin.
They say that five kinds of falsehoods are not sinful. ||36||
If, for the sake of their own kin, or for the sake of wealth, or out of partiality, they speak of what ought to be done,
they [dishonor] the ancestors of that lineage and family.
They cause even those who are established in heaven to fall. "They cause them to fall" means [they cast them down]. ||37||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra. ||16||
In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality, provided that he beholds the face of his born son while he is still living. (1)
"Infinite are the worlds for those with sons; there is no world for one without a son—so it is heard. (2)
"May they be childless and devourers," such is the curse. "O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality"—there is also a Vedic verse (nigama) thus.
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun. (5)
They dispute whether the son belongs to the owner of the field or to the progenitor; regarding this, they cite examples for both positions.
If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong only to the owners of the cows; the bull's exertion was in vain. (8)
Be vigilant and guard this lineage; let not others sow their seed in your field.
In the life hereafter, a son belongs to the one who begat him.
"Thus the knower weaves this web in vain. ||9||
When many men born of the same father have but one son,
the Vedic tradition declares that they all possess a son through that one son.
If among many wives who share one husband, even one has a son,
the sacred tradition (śruti) declares that they all possess sons by virtue of that son.
Thus, there are twelve sons as seen in the ancient tradition. The first is the one begotten by oneself on one's own consecrated wife.
In the absence of that, the son born of an appointed woman is the second. ||14||

The third [type of] appointed daughter (*putrikā*). It is understood that one who has no brother goes to the ancestors of the man [she marries]; she goes back [to her own kin] to attain the status of a son. Regarding this, there is a verse:
"I shall give you this unbrothered maiden, adorned; whatever son is born of her, he shall be my son. (15–17)

The fourth is the *paunarbhava* (woman remarried). ||18|| A *punarbhū* is one who, having abandoned her husband from her youth (*kaumāra*) and lived with others, returns to that very same man's household; she becomes a *punarbhū*. ||19|| Or, she who abandons a husband who is impotent, fallen, or insane, and finds another husband, or does so after he has died, she becomes a *punarbhū*. ||20||

The fifth is the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna). [21] He whom an unmarried woman, while in her father’s house, may bring forth through lust, is called a kānīna; they say he is the son of his maternal grandfather. [22] Furthermore, they cite this: "If an unmarried daughter of someone should obtain a son from a man of equal status, by that son the maternal grandfather becomes possessed of a son; he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth. [23]
And the one secretly born in the house is the sixth. Thus, these are said to be the heirs, kinsmen, and saviors from great danger.

Now, among those who have no heirs, the son born of a woman taken while pregnant (*sahoḍha*) is the first [in order of inheritance]. (26) He who is born of a woman who is married while already pregnant becomes a *sahoḍha* son. (27)
The second is the adopted son (dattaka). [28] He is one whom his parents may give away. [29]
The third [type of slave] is one who has been purchased. This has been explained by means of the story of Śunaḥśepa. King Hariścandra, it is said, purchased the son of Ajīgarta Sauyavasi.

The fourth [type of son] is one who comes of his own accord. This has been explained by means of the story of Śunaḥśepa. Indeed, Śunaḥśepa, when bound to the sacrificial post, praised the deities. The deities thereupon released his bonds. The officiating priests said, "Let this man be the son of me alone. He did not agree to them. They then reached an agreement, saying, "Let him be the son of whomever he desires. Viśvāmitra was his *hotṛ* priest; thus he attained the status of his son.
The fifth is the discarded son (apaviddha). [36] He is one whom one might adopt after he has been cast off by his mother and father. [37]

They say that the son of a Śūdra woman alone is the sixth [in this enumeration]. Thus, these are the kinsmen who do not inherit. Now they also cite this: "If among his six ancestors there should be no one at all who is an heir, these [six sons] shall take his inheritance."

Now follows the division of inheritance among brothers. (40) And those women who are childless [shall remain under their guardianship] until the birth of a son. (41) The eldest shall take two shares. (42) And from the cattle and horses, he shall take the tenth part. (43) Goats, sheep, and the house belong to the youngest. (44) Iron implements and household utensils belong to the middlemost.
