(45) The mother’s personal jewelry the women shall divide among themselves. (46)

If a Brāhmaṇa has sons by a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, and a Vaiśyā wife: ||47|| the son of the Brāhmaṇī shall take three shares; ||48|| the son of the Rājanyā (Kṣatriyā) shall take two shares; ||49|| the others shall divide the remainder equally. ||50||

And he by whom this [property] was produced himself shall take two shares. (51) But those who have entered another stage of life (āśrama) are entitled to no share. (52) So too are the impotent, the insane, and the outcaste. (53) However, there must be maintenance for the impotent and the insane. (54)

The wife of a deceased man shall observe a vow for six months, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, and sleeping on the ground. (55) After the six months have passed, she shall bathe, offer a *śrāddha* for her husband, and assemble those related by learning, ritual, teacher, or kinship; then her father or brother shall arrange the *niyoga*. (56) He shall not appoint a woman who is insane, lacking self-control, or diseased. (57) Nor one who is older [than the widower]. (58) [He shall wait] sixteen years, (59) unless he be afflicted by disease. (60)

During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, she should behave toward him as if he were her husband, except for laughing with him, harshness of speech, and physical violence. She should be the first to go to [the house] for food, clothing, bathing, and the application of unguents.

They say that when [a son] is born to a woman who has not been authorized, he becomes the son of the one who procreates him. (63) This would be so if there were two who are authorized. (64) There is no authorization due to greed for inheritance. (65) Some say that one may authorize [her] after having prescribed an expiation. (66)
A maiden who has reached puberty shall wait for three years. After those three years have passed, she may choose a husband of equal status. Furthermore, they cite this example:
"If, through the negligence of her father, a maiden here passes the proper age for marriage before being given away..."
Waiting expectantly, she destroys the giver,
like a heavy sacrificial fee paid when the time has passed.
Out of fear of the onset of puberty, the father should give away his daughter while she is still a maiden;
for if she remains until she has reached her menses, the blame falls upon the father. (70)
As many seasons as touch a maiden who, being of equal status and desirous, is being courted by [a suitor],
so many embryos have been killed by those two.
"From the mother and father"—this is the declaration of the Dharma. ||71||
If the groom should die first after she has been given by means of water and speech,
but before she has been led away by the mantras, the maiden belongs to her father alone.

If a maiden has been carried off by force, provided she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras, she may be given to another according to the prescribed rite; for she remains just as a maiden. (73)
If the husband has died while the young woman has been consecrated by the mere mantras, she, provided her womb remains intact, deserves to undergo the marriage rite again. (74)

A wife whose husband is away on a journey shall wait for five years. After five years have passed, she may go to her husband’s presence. If she is not willing to go because of religious or economic reasons, she should behave as if he were dead. Thus it is for a Brāhmaṇa woman: five years if she has borne children, four if she has not; for a Kṣatriya woman: five if she has borne children, three if she has not; for a Vaiśya woman: four if she has borne children, two if she has not; for a Śūdra woman: three if she has borne children, one if she has not.

From this point forward, among those who share the same purpose, birth, funeral rice-ball offerings, water libations, or lineage, each preceding one is more venerable than the next. However, as long as a member of one's own family is available, the succession should not pass to another.

If none of the six preceding [relatives] has any heir—neither a *sapiṇḍa* nor one who stands in the place of a son—his wealth they shall divide. (81) In their absence, the teacher and the pupil shall take it. (82) In their absence, the king shall take it. (83) But the king shall not take the property of a Brāhmaṇa. (84) For the property of a Brāhmaṇa is a terrible poison. (85)
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons. ||86||
One should bestow [it] upon those virtuous ones who have mastered the three Vedas; one should not bestow it otherwise. ||87||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

They say that one born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Caṇḍāla (1). From a Kṣatriya [father] and a Brāhmaṇī [mother], a Vaiṇa is born (2); from a Vaiśya [father] and a Brāhmaṇī [mother], an Antyāvasāyin (3). They say that one born of a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Rāmaka (4); from a Kṣatriya [father] and a Brāhmaṇī [mother], a Pulkasa (5). They say that one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Sūta (6). Furthermore, they cite this:

"Whatever offspring are born in secret, having resorted to the qualities of the inverse order (prātilomya), one should recognize them by their actions, due to their deviation from virtuous conduct" (7).

Those born from women one, two, or three classes lower than the fathers—namely, from a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya—become Ambaṣṭhas, Ugras, and Niṣādas respectively. From a Śūdra woman, he is a Pāraśava. They say that he is "already a corpse even while living" (pāram eva jīvan eva śavo bhavati). "Śava" is a designation for the dead.
Some indeed say that those who are Śūdras are this cremation ground. Therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra. Moreover, they cite these verses sung by Yama:
"Those Śūdras who are evildoers are this cremation ground manifest before our eyes;
therefore, one should never study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor the remains of food, nor that which has been prepared for a sacrificial oblation.
One should not instruct him in the Dharma, nor should one prescribe a vow to him. 14.
Whoever should teach him the Dharma, and whoever should prescribe a vow for him, he enters together with that person into a terrible, unmitigated darkness. ||15||
If a worm should ever appear in the opening of a wound, one is purified by a Prājāpatya penance; gold, a cow, or a garment is the sacrificial fee. ||16||
Having built the fire-altar, one should not approach a beautiful woman. A beautiful woman who is dark-complexioned is for pleasure alone, not for dharma; she is for pleasure alone, not for dharma.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

The king’s own duty is the protection of living beings; from its performance comes success. (1) The learned say that this sacrificial session (*sattram*) lasts until old age or death, and it involves the abandonment of both fear and compassion. (2) Therefore, among those duties fixed for the householder stage, he should appoint a domestic priest (*purohita*). (3) It is known [from scripture]: "A kingdom with a Brahmin as its domestic priest prospers. (4) This is because of the protection of both [the king and the subjects], (5) and also because of [the king's] incapacity [to perform all rites alone]. (6)

Having fully understood all the laws of the country, the laws of castes, and the laws of families, the king should establish the four social orders in their respective duties. He should inflict punishment upon those who deviate from them. Punishment, however, must be determined according to the specific circumstances of place, time, nature of the act, age, learning, and station; and it should be applied in cases of both physical injury and verbal abuse, based on sacred tradition and precedent.
One should not harm trees that bear flowers and fruit; however, one may cut them down for the purpose of cultivation or when they constitute a hindrance to domestic life.

The weights and measures shall be protected [from tampering]. (13) There shall be no mistreatment of caravans at their stations. (14) The price fixed by the market shall be the sole authority; there shall be no arbitrary imposition. (15) However, in the case of great festivals, there shall be no penalty and there shall be safety [for the merchants]. (16)

In a caravan, there should be a team of ten draft animals, providing double the labor [of a single animal]. (17) There should be water-stations at intervals. (18) A man should pull a load no less than one hundred [palas]. (19) Women should pull loads one and a half times [the weight] of men. (20)

Eight *māṣas* for a *tara* of medium quality; for one of inferior quality, it is one-quarter of a *kārṣāpaṇa*. (21) A *tara* of the lowest quality is worth one *māṣa*. (22) Exempt from toll are a learned *śrotriya*, a king’s servant, a person without a protector, a wandering ascetic, and those who are children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth. (23) Maidens traveling toward their future husbands and women whose children have died are also exempt. (24) If he carries [the goods] across with his own arms, he shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred times the amount. (25)

The burning of rivers, marshes, and forests, as well as the utilization of mountains, shall be free of taxes; or those who subsist upon them may pay [a fee]. However, one should cause a marriage-fee (*udvāhakara*) to be paid every month.

And when the king has died, one should provide for those who were dependent upon him. (29) By this, the conduct toward the mother is explained. (30) The king shall support the wives of his predecessor, as well as his paternal and maternal uncles. (31) Their daughters-in-law and other royal wives shall receive food and clothing; (32) or, if they do not desire it, they may enter the religious life. (33–34)
The king shall maintain those who are impotent or insane, because the inheritance belongs to them. Regarding the marriage-fee (*śulka*), they also cite this verse of Manu:
"There is no marriage-fee for a broken *kārṣāpaṇa* coin, nor for one engaged in a craft, nor for an infant, nor for an envoy."

Nor [is it forbidden] in what is obtained as alms, nor in what remains after being taken away, nor in the case of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), nor in the case of one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*), nor at a sacrifice (*yajña*). ||37||

A thief is not considered guilty if he has entered [the house] by a way other than the door. According to some, one who carries a weapon, one caught with the stolen goods, and one who bears wounds [from the act] are also [guilty]. When a man deserving punishment is released, the king shall fast for one night; the domestic priest (purohita) shall fast for three nights. When one undeserving of punishment is punished, the domestic priest shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance; the king shall fast for three nights. Furthermore, they cite this: "The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of the food; an unfaithful wife to her husband; a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king."
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds. ||45||

The king incurs no guilt if he causes one who has committed an offense to be executed according to the law of punishment, provided that the offender was caught in the act while abandoning his crime. ||46||
For kings, immediate purification is prescribed in matters of urgency;
likewise, in non-urgent matters, it is always time itself that is the determining factor. //47//
And regarding this, they cite the verse from the Yamagīta:
"There is no fault today for kings, nor indeed for those observing vows or performing sacrificial sessions;
for, seated in the station of Indra, they are eternally become Brahman."
For that [nature] of yours is eternal. ||48||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Expiation is required for an offense committed unintentionally; according to some, it is also required for one committed intentionally.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor for those whose sins are concealed. ||3||

And in that case, having been overtaken by sunrise, he should remain standing during the day and mutter the Sāvitrī; likewise, having been overtaken by sunset, he should remain seated during the night. One with deformed nails or black teeth, however, should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights.

7. A younger brother who marries before his elder brother (parivitti) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then marry [another wife], and then enter the household life. 8. Now, the elder brother whose younger brother has married before him (parivividāna) shall perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances, give [the bride] back to that [younger brother], and then marry [another wife] and enter the household life again. 9. The husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried (agredidhiṣūpati) shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, then marry [another wife], and then enter the household life. 10. The husband of an elder sister whose younger sister is already married (didhiṣūpati) shall perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances and give [the bride] back to that [husband].

We shall explain the expiation for the slayer of a hero later [in section 11]. One who has forsaken the Veda, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, should again receive the Veda from a teacher.

One who has violated the bed of his guru shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, place them in his joined palms, and walk facing south; wherever he meets with an obstacle, there he shall remain until the dissolution of the world. Or, stripped naked and smeared with clarified butter, he shall embrace a red-hot iron image of a woman; it is known from scripture that by death he becomes purified. The same applies to the wives of a teacher’s son or pupil, as well as to women of one’s own uterine kin.

Having had sexual intercourse with a female friend of one’s guru, or with a woman who is not a suitable vessel for marriage, or with one who has fallen from her caste, one shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one-fourth of a year. (16) This same penance applies to eating the food of a Caṇḍāla or of those who have fallen from their caste; thereafter, however, there is a re-initiation, though there is an exemption from shaving and the other [requirements of initiation]. (17) Regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"Shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging alms, and the vows—these are omitted in the rite of re-initiation. (18)

In the case of drinking liquor, however, for consuming *asurā* or *surā* unintentionally, there shall be the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, followed by the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśa*) and a renewed consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). The same applies to the consumption of urine, feces, or semen.

If any twice-born man should drink water contained in a vessel that held liquor, he becomes pure after three nights by drinking the water of these: the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the palāśa, and the kuśa grass. ||21||
But for habitual consumption of liquor, a twice-born man shall drink it while it is red-hot like fire.
One becomes purified through death. ||22||

We shall now declare the penance for the slayer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*): having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a slayer of an embryo, as does one who kills an embryo whose sex is unknown. For embryos whose sex is unknown may turn out to be males; therefore, they offer oblations with mantras addressed to the male. The slayer of an embryo, having kindled the sacred fire, should offer oblations.
"I offer the body hairs to Death; with the body hairs, I clothe Death"—this is the first [offering].
"I offer the skin to Death; with the skin, I clothe Death"—this is the second.
"I offer the blood to Death; with the blood, I clothe Death"—this is the third.
"I offer flesh to Death; with flesh I clothe Death"—with this he offers the fourth oblation.
"I offer sinews to Death; with sinews I clothe Death"—with this he offers the fifth oblation. "I offer fat to Death; with fat I clothe Death"—with this he offers the sixth oblation.
"I offer the bones to Death; with the bones I clothe Death"—this is the seventh [offering].
"I offer the marrow to Death; with the marrow I clothe Death"—this is the eighth. Thus [ends the section]. 26.

For the sake of a king or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, he should cause himself to be slain facing the enemy in battle. It is known from tradition that one who has failed three times becomes purified. Or, having dedicated himself for twelve years, he shall dwell neither in a village nor in a forest; carrying a skull-topped staff and holding a begging bowl made of a skull, he shall wander for alms at seven houses where no invitation was previously requested, proclaiming his own deed: "O giver, give alms to a killer of an embryo."
For it is known from the Nirukta that "the sin indeed becomes less. Nevertheless, they cite this example:
"By saying 'you are fallen' to one who has fallen, or again 'you are a thief' to a thief, one incurs an equal fault through such speech; if it is false, one incurs double the fault. (29–30)
Likewise, having killed a Kṣatriya, one should perform [the penance] for eight years; six for a Vaiśya; and three for a Śūdra. (31–33)

Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an Ātreyī, as well as a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a Soma sacrifice; we shall now explain who an Ātreyī is: they say an Ātreyī is a woman who has her menses and has bathed after her period, for it is in her that future offspring is conceived.

For killing an Ātreyī woman, [the penance is] for injuring a Kṣatriya; ||37|| for injuring a Kṣatriya woman, [it is] for injuring a Vaiśya; ||38|| for injuring a Vaiśya woman, [it is] for injuring a Śūdra; ||39|| having killed a Śūdra woman, [one must perform the penance] for one year. ||40||

For stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa, one should dishevel his hair and run toward the king, saying: "I am a thief, O Lord; may you punish me. The king should give him a weapon made of Udumbara wood, with which he should take his own life. It is known from tradition that by death he becomes purified. (41) Alternatively, having shaved off all his hair and being anointed with clarified butter, he should burn himself starting from the feet in a fire of cow-dung. It is known from tradition that by death he becomes purified. (42) Moreover, they cite this:
"For those who have died before their time due to various sinful deeds..."
Furthermore, hear how it becomes a limb for those who have again entered a body. ||43||

A thief becomes one with deformed nails; a killer of a Brahmin becomes one with white leprosy; a drinker of liquor has black teeth; and one who violates the teacher’s bed suffers from skin disease. ||44||

And in the case of association with outcasts—whether by means of the Vedic thread or through marriage—one must renounce those portions of the inheritance received from them and shall not dwell with them. It is known from tradition that by going toward the northern direction, fasting, and studying the *Saṃhitā*, one becomes purified. Furthermore, they cite this:
"By mortification of the body, by austerity, and by study, the evildoer is released from evil; and by giving, he is likewise liberated."
Thus it is known; thus it is known. ||47||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red darbha grass and cast him into the fire. Having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head and having anointed her with clarified butter, she should be led naked upon a donkey along the high road. It is declared that she thus becomes purified. 2.

If a Kṣatriya should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head to be shaved and having anointed her with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a white donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. "She becomes purified," so it is known. 3.
In this same way, a Vaiśya [begets] on a Kṣatriya woman; and a Śūdra [begets] on Kṣatriya and Vaiśya women.

If a wife commits an infidelity against her husband through thought alone, she shall eat barley gruel or rice with milk for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights have passed, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra, each time accompanied by a prostration of the head. It is traditionally taught that she thereby becomes purified. 6.

Regarding the connection with speech: having performed this very [penance] for one month, after the month has passed, she should offer oblations with four hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī verse while submerged in water, using [four] heads [of a sacrificial animal]. It is known from tradition that she thus becomes purified.

In the case of sexual intercourse, however, she should wear a cloth soaked in ghee for one year; eating on a bed of cow-dung or a layer of *kuśa* grass, she should sleep on the ground. After one year has passed, she should offer oblations with her head submerged in water while reciting the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times. It is known from tradition that she thus becomes purified. (8)
But through sexual intercourse or visiting sacred fords, one turns away from the duties. ||9||
However, four [wives] must be abandoned: she who has gone to a disciple, she who has gone to a teacher, she who especially kills her husband, and she who has approached a degraded man.
The Brahmin woman who drinks liquor,
the gods do not lead her to the world of her husband; having exhausted her merit, she wanders right here in this very world.
Or it becomes a water-dwelling creature, such as a pearl oyster. ||11||
The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not.
They should perform the penance in reverse order, followed by the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.
For those women who are devoted to their husbands, who are householders, and who are firm in their vows of truth and purity,
their worlds are equal to those of their husbands.
The worlds of jackals are for those who are unfaithful. ||14||
Half of the body of that man falls [with him] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed. (15)

If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach the wife of another Brāhmaṇa, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance if the husband has ceased his religious duties, and the Atikṛcchra penance if he has not ceased them. The same applies to the wives of a Rājanya or a Vaiśya.
If he should kill a cow, he must remain wrapped in her raw hide for six months, performing either the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra* penance. This is the rule for those two.
For three days he eats during the day, and for three days he eats at night;
for three days he observes the vow of not asking for food, and for three days he does not eat at all.
Thus ends the Kṛcchra penance. ||20||
For three days one should drink warm water, for three days one should drink warm milk;
having drunk warm ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for the final three days.

Thus ends the Taptakṛcchra penance. [21] And in the case of killing a bull or a cow, one should give [a gift]. Moreover, they quote: "In ancient times there were only three diseases: envy, fasting, and old age;
having killed a spotted goat, one should bring back ninety-eight [goats]. [23]

Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a mouse, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift. (24) Having killed a heap of boneless creatures equal in size to a cow, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give some small gift. (25) But for each individual creature possessing bones, [the penance is the same]. (26)

He who casts away the sacred fires shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and then have the fires re-established. [27] If one has falsely accused his teacher, he shall bathe with his clothes on and propitiate the teacher; it is known from tradition that through such propitiation he becomes purified. [28] An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism. [29] But one who lives according to atheistic principles shall perform the *atikṛcchra*. [30] By this, the seller of Soma is also explained. [31]

A forest-dweller (vānaprastha), upon a breach of initiation, shall perform the twelve-night kṛcchra penance and then increase his growth in a great thicket of grass. For mendicants, the increase of the soma-growth is as for the forest-dweller, and there is the refinement according to their own scripture; and there is the refinement according to their own scripture.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

Now, this man indeed performs falsely: he either officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed, or he accepts what should not be accepted, or he eats what is not food, or he practices what should not be practiced. Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation, or should one not? They say: "One should not perform it," because "an action is not exhausted. But one should indeed perform it, because of the evidence of the Śruti: "He crosses over all evil, he crosses over even the murder of a Brahmin, who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha"; and "One who is accused should sacrifice with the Gosava and the Agniṣṭut."

The means of expiation for that are recitation (*japa*), austerity (*tapas*), burnt offerings (*homa*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and giving gifts (*dāna*). (8) The *Upaniṣads*, the beginning of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the *Saṃhitās* of all the Vedic meters, the honey-hymns (*madhu*), the *Aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the two *Sāmans* known as the *Rājana* and *Rauhiṇa*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns, the *Pāvamānī* verses, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers (*pāvana*). (9) Furthermore, they cite this: "By performing once at each season the sacrifice to Vaiśvānara, the *Vrātapatī*, and likewise the *Pavitreṣṭi*, one purifies ten generations of ancestors. (10)

According to the method of initiation, the following are purifying: the vow of subsisting on milk, eating fruits, barley-gruel from a handful, consuming gold, and drinking Soma (11). All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, dwellings of sages, cow-pens, and sacrificial enclosures are the appropriate places (12). A year, a month, twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, and a day and night are the appropriate times (13).

In cases where no specific rule is prescribed, these very [penances] may be performed optionally. For heavy sins, the penances are heavy; for light sins, they are light. The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation—the universal expiation.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he should sacrifice a donkey as an animal dedicated to the Rākṣasas in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest; or he should offer a sacrificial pap (*caru*) dedicated to Nirṛti. He should offer from it [the oblations]: "To Desire, svāhā! To him who desires desire, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities who are the Rākṣasas, svāhā! (1–3).
This same [penance applies] for the intentional emission of semen during the daytime, in dreams, or during other [periods of] vows, until the ritual of returning home (samāvartana). ||4||

For sexual intercourse with an animal, one should give a white bull with black genitals; for intercourse with a menstruating woman, one should give a black bull with white genitals. Having had intercourse with a cow, the offense is explained as being equal to the killing of a Śūdra.

For a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), there is a cessation of his vows upon performing the funeral rites for [a parent]. (7) Except in the case of [the death of] one's mother or father. (8)

If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remnants of his teacher's food for the sake of medicine. (9) If he should die while commissioned by the teacher, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances. (10)

If a religious student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat, he shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, which involves eating only the remnants of food, and then complete the remainder of his vow. (11) The same applies to eating at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*) or during periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*). (12) It is known from the Vājasaneyaka that honey obtained unintentionally does not cause defilement. (13)

If one who has been accused commits suicide, there is an interruption of the funeral rites for his sapinda relatives. (14) He who destroys himself by means of wood, water, a clod of earth, a stone, a weapon, poison, or a rope is considered a self-killer. (15) Furthermore, they cite this example:
"If a twice-born man, out of affection, should perform the funeral rites for one who has committed suicide, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow accompanied by the Taptakṛcchra penance. (16)
We shall explain the Cāndrāyaṇa penance later [in sūtra 20]. In the case of the resolve to commit suicide, the penance lasts for three nights.
One who abandons his life while still living shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights;
he must also fast for three nights and always wear a garment that is oiled.
Having restrained his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
or else, according to this same method, he should recite the Gāyatrī.
Alternatively, having established the sacred fire, one should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras;
by this, everything other than the great sins (mahāpātaka) is purified.

Moreover, he should sip water while reciting, "May Agni and Manyu... Having mentally contemplated evil during the morning, he should mutter the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*, or he should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. ||23||
Upon touching human bone that is oily, there is impurity for three nights; however, if it is not oily, there is impurity for one day and night. The same applies to following a corpse.

If one enters between those who are studying, there shall be fasting for a day and a night. [27] There shall be a three-night fast, ritual ablution, and mutual exile from one another. [28] In the case of dogs, cats, mongooses, or swift-moving creatures, there shall be fasting for a day and a night. [29]

For eating the flesh of dogs, chickens, village pigs, herons, vultures, eagles, pigeons, humans, crows, or owls, there shall be a fast for seven nights, becoming free of feces, consuming clarified butter, and undergoing the rite of re-consecration. 30.
A Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog becomes pure by going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and consuming clarified butter. ||31||
Time, fire, purity of mind, looking at water and the sun, and ignorance of [the faults of] living beings—these six kinds of purification are prescribed. ||32||
It is traditionally known that upon touching a dog, a Caṇḍāla, or an outcaste, one becomes pure immediately by bathing with one's clothes on. ||33||

Upon hearing of a fallen person, a *caṇḍāla*, or a corpse, they shall remain for three nights with speech restrained and without eating; so it is known. Or, by practicing that [recitation] up to a thousand times, they become pure; so it is known. By this very rule, those who teach what is censured and those who sacrifice for such persons are explained. And it is known that they become pure through the relinquishment of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

Now, furthermore, for the killing of an embryo, one should subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights. Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime causing loss of caste or of a crime not causing loss of caste, one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the Śuddhavatī verses. Or, one should go to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). By this, the case of one who has been falsely accused is explained.

[Furthermore, regarding sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached: one should subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights; or one should go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). By this very rule, sexual intercourse with a *caṇḍāla* woman is explained. ||41||
Now follows another general method for the Kṛcchra penance, arranged in an expanded form. ||42||
One day in the morning, one day at night, and one day without begging;
one day of the *parāka* penance—thus two further four-day periods.
For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma, likewise prescribed the Śiśukṛcchra for children, the elderly, and the sick. 43.
Now follows the procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. ||44||
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
consuming while gradually decreasing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In the same way, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, he should consume another morsel;
eating while increasing the number of morsels, he should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In this very place, one should chant the Sāmans, or else mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
This month-long Cāndrāyaṇa penance is a purifier praised by the sages;
it is prescribed as an expiation for all those cases where no specific penance has been ordained.
It is prescribed. ||47||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.

Now follows the *atikṛcchra* (exceedingly difficult penance). [1] Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening, and eating only what is unasked for during the *parāka*—this is the *kṛcchra*. One should eat as much as one might take in a single [mouthful]; that, according to the previous rule, is the *atikṛcchra*. [2]
Subsisting on water is the *kṛcchra*; that [same practice] is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. ||3||

The forms of the *kṛcchra* penances are as follows: [4] He should have his beard and hair shaved, except for the eyebrows, eyelashes, and the top-knot (*śikhā*); having trimmed his nails, wearing a single garment, eating blameless food, he should beg for alms once, bathe at the three times of day, carry a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), avoid conversation with women and *śūdras*, and practice standing and sitting postures; during the day he should stand, and at night he should sit. [5]

Thus spoke the Blessed Vasiṣṭha: "The Dharmaśāstra that has been proclaimed by the virtuous should not be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not resided [with the teacher] for a year. A thousand [cows] as a sacrificial fee, with a bull as the eleventh, or the favor of the teacher—yes, the favor of the teacher. (6–7)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
I shall describe, without omission, the purification for all great sins whose faults have not been publicly proclaimed, as well as for all minor offenses.

For one who has maintained the sacred fires, for the disciplined, the elderly, or even the learned, the penance is that which is declared in secret; other people [should perform] that which was previously mentioned. ||2||
Those who are constantly disciplined through purifying breath-control, gifts, burnt offerings, and recitations are liberated from their transgressions; of this there is no doubt. (3)

Seated with the sacred thread (pavitra) in hand, one should practice the daily Vedic recitation (brahma), as well as breath-control (prāṇāyāma), the purificatory syllables (pavitrāṇi), the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava.
Constantly engaged and repeatedly practicing breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), let him perform supreme austerity from the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails. (5)
From cessation wind is born; from wind, fire is indeed born;
from heat, water is then born; thus it is purified within by these three.
O twice-born ones, that state which they attain through yoga cannot be reached by means of intense austerity, nor by Vedic study, nor by sacrifice. (7)
Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Yoga is eternal supreme austerity; therefore, one should always be disciplined in yoga. (8)
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, in the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
and in the three-footed *gāyatrī*, no fear exists anywhere.
Likewise, the Vedas, beginning with the Praṇava, are established within the Praṇava;
the Praṇava is the entirety of speech. Therefore, one should practice the Praṇava. ||10||
The single syllable is known as the supreme Brahman, the ultimate purifier. ||11||
When a mixture of all kinds of sins has occurred,
the great purification is ten thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī mantra.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
That is what is called [the "one who has been spoken of"]. ||13||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
He who, unwearied, performs three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the rule, destroys in that very instant the sin committed during a day and night. ||1||
Sitting during the evening twilight, one dispels through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) whatever sin has been committed during the day by deed, mind, or speech. ||2||
Whatever sin has been committed by deed, thought, or word during the night,
one dispels it by means of breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) upon rising for the morning twilight devotion.
He who restrains himself again and again through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) should, O supreme ascetic, perform meditation for two, three, or even double that duration. (3)
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava, performed day after day, purify even the slayer of an embryo within a month. (4)
Having recited this [hymn] of Kautsa, as well as the triplet belonging to Vasiṣṭha,
the Māhitra, and the Śuddhavatīs, even a drinker of spirituous liquor is purified.
By reciting the Āsyavāmīya and the Śivasaṃkalpa even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant, even after having stolen gold.
By practicing the *haviṣyantīya* hymn and the verse beginning with "na tamaṃhaḥ," and by reciting the *puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the Guru’s bed is liberated. (7)
Or else, while submerged in water, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
Manu has declared that it is equal to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) at the end of a horse sacrifice.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (ārambhayajña);
the whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold, and the mental (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña),
are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin. (11)

Sins do not dwell among those who recite prayers, those who perform fire-sacrifices, those who practice meditation, those who reside at sacred fords, and those who have bathed while observing the head-vow.
Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
even so a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly devoted to silent recitation shines forth brilliantly.
For those who constantly study their own sacred texts, who are ever self-restrained, and who likewise mutter prayers and offer oblations, no downfall exists. 14.
One who desires purification should employ this goddess consisting of a thousand verses at most, a hundred in the middle, and ten at the least, even if one is situated in all manner of sins. 15.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own adversity through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through prayers and fire-offerings.
Just as horses would be without a chariot, or a chariot without horses, so too is austerity for one lacking knowledge, or knowledge for one who lacks austerity. (17)
Just as food joined with honey, or honey joined with food, so too are austerity and knowledge together a great medicine. (18)
Sin does not attach itself even to a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly engaged in silent recitation, provided he is endowed with knowledge and austerity, even if he has committed evil deeds.
This is not applicable. ||19||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Even if more than a hundred misdeeds have been committed, if the Veda is retained in memory, the fire of that person’s knowledge consumes them all, just as fire consumes fuel. (1)
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees, so does the fire of knowledge burn away the defects of the self born of karma. ||2||
Even having slain these worlds and consuming [their wealth] here and there,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
One should not take delight in evil deeds by relying on the power of the Vedas;
for it is through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by karma, and not otherwise. //4//
The sage who performs austerities in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and he who studies even a single verse of the Veda—these two are equal. (5)
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me. (6)
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability and the performance of the sequence of the great sacrifices quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes. //7//
One should constantly perform one's own duty as declared in the Vedas without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal. (8)

From officiating at sacrifices, from teaching, from matrimonial alliance, and likewise from accepting improper gifts—no fault shall accrue to him regarding Brahmins, for he is equal to fire and the sun. //9//
When a cause for suspicion has arisen regarding what is considered unfit to be eaten or consumed, I shall declare the purification of food; listen to me as I speak.
A Brahmin should drink the bitter, salt-free *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*,
as well as *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, along with milk for three nights.
Having boiled the leaves of the *palāśa* and *bilva*, *kuśa* grass, lotuses, and *udumbara* fruits, one should drink the water; thus one becomes pure in just three nights.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass,
along with a one-night fast, would purify even a dog-eater (outcaste).
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
taking these as one's food for five nights, one is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
One who employs barley according to the prescribed rule is purified by direct perception itself;
when the state of being is pure, all things become pure, but if it is impure, they remain stained with passion.
Three morning meals of sacrificial food, and likewise three evening meals,
as well as three meals of unsolicited food— this shall constitute a three-day fast.
If, however, the wind-eater (the ascetic) hastens to perform it during the day,
having stayed in the water throughout the night until dawn, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times when the sun has risen, one is liberated from all sins, provided that one is not a slayer of a Brahmin. (18)
Indeed, whether one is a thief, a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, or a violator of the guru’s bed, by merely studying the Dharmaśāstra, one is liberated from all sins. (19)
The Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances indeed destroy all sins—those that are difficult to overcome, those resulting from improper performance of rites, as well as great evils. (20)
One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
on the new moon day, one should not eat at all—such is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
And thus is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. ||21||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.
A woman is not defiled by a paramour, nor a Brahmin by Vedic rituals;
water is not defiled by urine or feces, nor fire by the act of burning.
Whether she has herself consented, or has been driven away, or has been enjoyed by force, or has even fallen into the hands of thieves; (2)
A defiled woman is not to be abandoned; her abandonment is not prescribed. One should wait for her period of menstruation; she becomes pure through the time of her menses. ||3||
Women are an incomparable purifier; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
they subsequently go to human beings, yet they are not defiled according to dharma. ||5||
Soma gave them purity, Gandharva taught them speech, and Agni granted them the power to consume all things; therefore, women are free from blemish.
Those who know the Dharma recognize three sins for a woman in this world:
the killing of her husband, the destruction of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus. (7)
A calf is pure when causing milk to flow; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; women are pure during sexual union; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
Goats and horses are pure in their mouths; cows are pure in their backs;
Brahmins are pure in their feet; but women are pure in every way.
Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by whose recitations and burnt offerings people are purified; of this there is no doubt. (10)
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānīs, and the Durgā-sāvitrī; ||11||
The Atīṣaṅgas, the Padastobhas, the Sāmans, as well as the Vyāhṛtis, the Bhāruṇḍa Sāmans, the Gāyatra, and likewise the Raivata; ||12||
The Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa, as well as the Devavratas; the Abliṅga, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and likewise the Madhvṛcas. ||13||
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Triṣuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans, the Śuddha and the Aśuddhi. (14)
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Vrata of Agni, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these, when recited, purify living beings.
If he so desires, he attains the recollection of his past births. ||15||
Gold is the first offspring of Agni;
the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun;
may one enjoy the infinite fruit of these.
He who would give gold, a cow, and land; ||16||
A cow, a horse, gold, or land obstruct the donor when they see the hand of a Brahmin who is devoid of Vedic learning and has been expelled from his community. (17)
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should offer seven or five Brahmins black sesame seeds—or otherwise [white ones]—mixed with honey. (18)
"May Dharmarāja be pleased"—whatever such thought dwells in one's mind, even the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment. (19)
Having fashioned a black antelope with its hooves intact and a golden navel, one who covers it with sesame seeds and gives it away—listen to the fruit of his merit. (20)
By him, the earth—with its golden caves, its mountains, forests, and groves, and its four faces—would have been given; of this there is no doubt. (21)
"He who places sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin and gives gold, honey, and clarified butter to a Brahmin, overcomes all evil deeds."
One overcomes all evil deeds. ||22||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Through generosity, one obtains all desires; through celibacy, one attains long life and beauty.

By practicing non-violence, one attains heaven. ||3|| By entering the fire, one reaches the world of Brahmā. ||4|| Through silence, one gains good fortune. ||5|| By dwelling in water, one becomes the lord of the Nāgas. ||6||

One who gives medicine becomes free from disease and has his afflictions exhausted. ||7|| A giver of water becomes enriched with all desires. ||8|| A giver of food becomes endowed with clear vision and mindfulness. ||9|| An intelligent person who gives freedom from fear in every way [attains the same]. ||10|| By giving a vehicle yoked with oxen, one obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords (tīrtha). ||11|| From the gift of a bed and a seat, one gains lordship over the inner apartments. ||12|| From the gift of an umbrella, one gains a house. ||13|| A giver of a house attains a city. ||14|| A giver of sandals obtains a vehicle. ||15||
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Whatever sin a man oppressed by his livelihood may commit, he is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cow-hide. (16)
One should give a full water-pot to a Brahmin for the purpose of sipping;
having attained supreme satisfaction after death, he is born again as a drinker of Soma.
The gift of thousands of oxen, capable of bearing the yoke,
given according to the rules to a worthy recipient, is equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and Sarasvatī;
for among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is indeed superior to them. (19)
The wise person who, free from malice, follows this conduct—which bestows the ultimate fruit and liberates one from both saṃsāra and mokṣa—[attains that goal]. (20)
One who is faithful, pure, and self-controlled should either uphold or even hear this; having abandoned all sins, he is honored upon the back of heaven.
"He is honored on the back of the vault of heaven. ||21||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
Practice Dharma, not non-Dharma; speak the truth, not falsehood.
Look to the long-term, not the short-term; look to the ultimate, not the immediate. (1)

The Brahmin is Agni. (2) For there is a Vedic revelation: "Agni, indeed, is the Brahmin. (3) And how is that so? (4) In this regard, the *sadas* is the body of the Brahmin; the altar (*vedi*) is his resolve; the sacrifice is his animal victim; the tethering rope is his intellect; the *sadas* is his mouth; the *āhavanīya* fire is his navel; the *gārhapatya* fire is his stomach; the *adhvaryu* priest is his out-breath (*prāṇa*); the *hotṛ* priest is his in-breath (*apāna*); the *brahmā* priest is his diffused breath (*vyāna*); the *udgātṛ* priest is his equalized breath (*samāna*); the self and the senses are the sacrificial vessels. He who, knowing thus, offers the objects of the senses with the senses—this is also known in the *Kaṭhaka*. (5)
Moreover, they cite this example:
"An offering poured into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins—fires enriched by the fuel of the Vedas—protects and saves both the giver and himself from sin. (6)
That which does not spill over, does not cause distress, and does not bring reproach—this offering made into the mouth of a Brahmin is superior even to the Agnihotra sacrifice. (7)
The fire is meditation, the piling of fuel is truth, the oblation is patience,
the sacrificial ladle is modesty, the sacrificial cake is non-violence, the post is contentment,
and the gift for the beings is the granting of fearlessness.
Having performed a mental sacrifice, the wise man goes to his end.
The hair of an aging person decays; the teeth of an aging person decay;
but the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay even as one ages. (9)

"That which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays, and which is a disease that ends only with life—that craving, for one who abandons it, there is happiness. (10)
Homage be to Vasiṣṭha, the son of Urvaśī, born of Mitra and Varuṇa, the one who has a hundred ways; to Vasiṣṭha! ||11||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Vasiṣṭha-dharmaśāstra.
And thus concludes this Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Dharmaśāstra.
